meta.title: Who really said "The reasonable man adapts himself to the world; the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — it’s George Bernard Shaw, from “Maxims for Revolutionists” in Man and Superman (1903). The popular version drops his punchline about progress.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The reasonable man adapts himself to the world; the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: George Bernard Shaw wrote it in “Maxims for Revolutionists,” appended to Man and Superman (1903). The famous cut drops “all progress depends on the unreasonable man.”

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Shaw wrote this as a maxim under the heading “Reason” in “Maxims for Revolutionists,” the aphorism appendix to his 1903 play Man and Superman. The wording is confirmed against the printed text; the widely-quoted form simply drops his concluding line, “Therefore all progress depends on the unreasonable man.”

source.excerpt: The reasonable man adapts himself to the world: the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself. Therefore all progress depends on the unreasonable man.
trail: Confirmed word-for-word in the “Reason” maxims of Shaw’s “Maxims for Revolutionists” ↗, the appendix to Man and Superman.
Sourced to the same work, section and 1903 date by WIST Quotations ↗.
Man and Superman was written 1901–1903 and first published in 1903, placing the text firmly in the public domain.
source.cutTag: ↑ the popular version stops early and swaps Shaw’s colon for a semicolon
source.excerptNote: Shaw’s original uses a colon after “the world,” and the maxim doesn’t end where it’s usually quoted — his real point is the third sentence, that “all progress depends on the unreasonable man.”

author.bio: George Bernard Shaw (1856–1950) was an Irish-born playwright, critic and polemicist, and a leading figure in the Fabian socialist movement. Man and Superman (1903) is among his best-known plays, and the “Maxims for Revolutionists” appended to it are a rich source of his aphorisms. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1925.

context.heading: Shaw’s point about progress
lead: Shaw framed the maxim as a defense of the awkward, uncompromising reformer. Its force lives in the sentence usually left off: because the “unreasonable” person refuses to accommodate the world as it is, “all progress depends on the unreasonable man.”
detailsBody: The circulating version typically replaces Shaw’s colon with a semicolon and stops after “to himself,” turning a three-part argument into a tidy contrast. Quoting the full maxim restores Shaw’s actual thesis about who drives change.
